Murray–Goulburn | nativename = | region = [[Victoria (Australia)|Victoria]], [[Australia]] | ethnicity = [[Yorta Yorta]] ([[Pangerang]], [[Kwatkwat]]) | extinct = by 1960 | ref = | revived = 151 self-identified speakers (2021 census){{Cite web|url=https://www.abs.gov.au/statistics/people/people-and-communities/cultural-diversity-census/2021/|title=Cultural diversity: Census|author=Australian Bureau of Statistics|access-date=13 October 2022|date=2021}} | familycolor = Australian | fam1 = [[Pama–Nyungan languages|Pama–Nyungan]] | fam2 = [[Yotayotic languages|Yotayotic]] | dia1 = Yaliba-Yaliba | iso3 = xyy | glotto = yort1237 | glottorefname = Yorta Yorta | aiatsis = D2 }} '''Yorta Yorta''' (Yotayota) is a [[dialect cluster]], or perhaps a group of closely related languages, spoken by the [[Yorta Yorta people]], [[Indigenous Australian]]s from the junction of the [[Goulburn River (Victoria)|Goulburn]] and [[Murray River]]s in present-day northeast [[Victoria, Australia|Victoria]]. [[R. M. W. Dixon|Dixon]] considers it an [[language isolate|isolate]]. Yorta Yorta clans include the [[Bangerang]], Kailtheban, Wollithiga, Moira, Penrith, Ulupna, [[Kwat Kwat]] and Nguaria-iiliam-wurrung.[http://www.dse.vic.gov.au/dse/nrenlwm.nsf/LinkView/7FA349BEAE0F5A3FCA256E8D00210309A4AD52AC7C448F1A4A256DEA0024EDD2 Yorta Yorta Co-operative Management Agreement] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060913195148/http://www.dse.vic.gov.au/dse/nrenlwm.nsf/LinkView/7FA349BEAE0F5A3FCA256E8D00210309A4AD52AC7C448F1A4A256DEA0024EDD2 |date=September 13, 2006 }} The name is also spelled ''Jotijota, Jodajoda, Joti-jota, Yodayod, Yoda-Yoda, Yoorta, Yota, Yoti Yoti, Yotta-Yotta, Youta''; other names are '' Arramouro, Boonegatha, Echuca, Gunbowerooranditchgoole, Gunbowers, Kwart Kwart, Unungun, Wol-lithiga ~ Woollathura''. The Yaliba Yaliba language of the Pikkolaatpan tribe is about 70% similar to the dialect of the Bangerang, suggesting they may be closely related languages rather than dialects. == Revival == Although the language is considered dormant due to contact with Europeans and forcible dislocation to missions, the Yorta Yorta have maintained many words. There have been strong moves of late to revive the language. Two Yorta Yorta women, Lois Peeler and Sharon Atkinson, together with Dr Heather Bowe from [[Monash University]], worked for several years to compile a comprehensive record of research material, entitled ''Yorta Yorta Language Heritage''. This work provided a summary of existing written records, with reference to the spoken resources, and included introductory lessons in Yorta Yorta, together with English to Yorta Yorta and Yorta Yorta to English dictionaries. == Phonology == === Consonants === {| class="wikitable" ! ![[Bilabial consonant|Labial]] ![[Dental consonant|Dental]] ![[Alveolar consonant|Alveolar]] ![[Palatal consonant|Palatal]] ![[Retroflex consonant|Retroflex]] ![[Velar consonant|Velar]] |- align="center" ![[Stop consonant|Stop]] |{{IPA link|b}} |{{IPA link|d̪}} |{{IPA link|d}} |{{IPA link|ɟ}} |({{IPA link|ɖ}}) |{{IPA link|ɡ}} |- align="center" ![[Nasal consonant|Nasal]] |{{IPA link|m}} |{{IPA link|n̪}} |{{IPA link|n}} |{{IPA link|ɲ}} |({{IPA link|ɳ}}) |{{IPA link|ŋ}} |- align="center" ![[Lateral consonant|Lateral]] | | |{{IPA link|l}} |({{IPA link|ʎ}}) |({{IPA link|ɭ}}) | |- align="center" ![[Rhotic consonant|Rhotic]] | | |{{IPA link|ɾ}}~{{IPA link|r}} | |({{IPA link|ɽ}}) | |- align="center" ![[Approximant consonant|Approximant]] |{{IPA link|w}} | | |{{IPA link|j}} | | |} A palatal lateral or the following retroflex consonants could have potentially been recorded. There are vowel-initial words Yorta-Yorta, due to the deletion of {{IPA|[j]}} or sometimes {{IPA|[ŋ]}} before {{IPA|[a]}}, but not in Yabula-Yabula. ==Music== [[File:Jessica Mauboy at Mbantua Festival.jpg|thumb|left|250px|Indigenous pop, R&B, and soul singer [[Jessica Mauboy]] performs "[[Ngarra Burra Ferra]]" at the 2013 Mbantua Festival in [[Alice Springs, Northern Territory]], with [[Aboriginal Australian]] students from Yipirinya State Primary School, of which Mauboy is the official ambassador.]] The track "[[Ngarra Burra Ferra]]" sung by indigenous artist [[Jessica Mauboy]] from the 2012 hit film ''[[The Sapphires (film)|The Sapphires]]'' is a song based on the traditional [[Aboriginal Australians|Aboriginal]] hymn "Bura Fera".{{cite web|url=http://towalkwithyou.com/the-lyrics-to-bura-fera/|title=The lyrics to Bura Fera|publisher=towalkwithyou.com|date=13 September 2013|access-date=26 April 2014|archive-date=10 April 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170410143250/http://towalkwithyou.com/the-lyrics-to-bura-fera/|url-status=dead}} The song is in the Yorta Yorta language and speaks of the Lord [[God]]'s help in decimating a [[Pharaoh]]'s armies. The chorus, {{lang|xyy|Ngara burra ferra yumini yala yala}}, translates into English as "The Lord God drowned all Pharaoh's armies, hallelujah!" These lyrics are based on an ancient song in [[Jewish]] tradition known as the "Song of the Sea" or "Miriam's Song", as it was composed and sung by [[Miriam]], older sister of the prophet [[Moses]]. It can be found in [[Exodus 15]], especially verse 4: "Pharaoh's chariots and his host hath he cast into the sea: his chosen captains also are drowned in the Red Sea." Aboriginal communities of Victoria and southern [[New South Wales]] may be the only people in the world who still sing the piece (in Yorta Yorta). {{clear}} ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== *Federation of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Languages (FATSIL), [https://web.archive.org/web/20061012231600/http://www.fatsil.org/LOTM/oct99.htm Language of the Month: Yorta Yorta [Victoria]], 1999 * [http://www.lib.monash.edu/collections/monash-authors/pre2000/0858835134.html Monash University Library] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120206010224/http://www.lib.monash.edu/collections/monash-authors/pre2000/0858835134.html |date=2012-02-06 }} * [http://aiatsis.gov.au/sites/default/files/docs/collections/language_bibs/bangerang_kwat_kwat_waveroo.pdf Bibliography of Bangerang language and people resources] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150518092512/http://aiatsis.gov.au/sites/default/files/docs/collections/language_bibs/bangerang_kwat_kwat_waveroo.pdf |date=2015-05-18 }}, at the [[Australian Institute of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Studies]] {{Pama–Nyungan languages|South}} {{Authority control}} [[Category:Yotayotic languages]] [[Category:Yorta Yorta]]
